The story has a strong underlying unity that binds its setting, plot, and character reflections into a cohesive whole. The inciting incident—finding a deceased woman at the scene of a car crash on an isolated, indifferent mountain road—logically sets up the middle of the story, where Martin is forced to wait and begins speaking to the woman to fill the silence and make the vast world feel "human-sized again." His seemingly disparate memories (his dog Edgar, his two ex-wives, and his career as a city planner) are all deeply interconnected by the central themes of loneliness, the weight of memory, and the realization of what truly matters after an ending occurs. Even his past profession of designing roads and his failure to acknowledge a woman's ruined garden directly echo his present situation: standing on a crumbling road, determined not to abandon a stranger. Finally, the ending brings all these threads together in a quiet, reflective resolution as he stays with her until help arrives.
